results.title: What's new in Foundry Agent Service at Ignite 2026 | Microsoft Foundry Blog
excerpts:
Operate them with confidence by turning production evidence into validated improvements. Here’s what’s new, and how each capability helps you move from idea to impact.

Build: Create agents on your terms

Build harness agents with the tools you use

The Microsoft Copilot harness , in public preview, gives developers a fully managed way to build prompt agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox; you bring the knowledge, reusable skills, and connected tools that make the agent yours. Instead of rebuilding execution machinery, your team can focus on the agent’s expertise and results.
Author Copilot harness agents in the Foundry UI, the GitHub Copilot app, the Foundry CLI (azd ai), or the Foundry Toolkit for VS Code, and keep agent definitions in source control alongside your application code. [Read what’s new in Foundry dev tools →]
You can choose the right starting point for your application: author a prompt agent using the Microsoft Copilot harness, or bring your own code and orchestration through hosted agents. Foundry Agent Service supports those choices without requiring every team to use the same framework or take the same approach to agent logic.
What’s new in Foundry Agent Service at Ignite 2026

Voice conversations to your agents, now generally available

Talking to AI should feel as natural as talking to a person. Voice agents in Foundry Agent Service are now generally available, giving organizations an enterprise-grade way to add real-time voice to their agents. That covers serving customers, supporting employees, and powering in-car and in-app assistants.

...

At Ignite, we’re expanding how Foundry agents connect to tools, business context, and other agents. Work IQ and Fabric IQ integrations, in preview, bring Microsoft 365 context and Fabric data into agent workflows. Web Search powered by Web IQ is generally available for prompt agents, with Toolbox support coming soon, while the generally available A2A tool connects Foundry and external agents. Toolboxes make these capabilities reusable through a managed MCP endpoint, with expanded skills support, a monitoring dashboard, and preview tool policies.
Computer use and browser automation are now generally available for tasks that require an application interface rather than an API. Browser automation combines isolated browser sessions with Live View and Take control for human oversight, session recordings in customer-owned storage, and preview access to applications behind private virtual networks. [Read what’s new in tools and toolboxes in Foundry →]

Deploy: Put agents to work at scale

Run hosted agents with less friction

Hosted agents let you bring your application code and orchestration to a managed runtime. At Ignite, we’re expanding scale, enterprise controls, and deployment choice:
* Shared subnet IPs — GA: Sessions share subnet IP addresses while retaining their own VM-isolated sandboxes, reducing pressure on private IP capacity. Default quotas are 1,000–2,000 concurrent sessions per subscription and region, with increases available on request.
* Memory snapshots — Public preview: Reduce cold starts by restoring an initialized agent state instead of repeatedly loading libraries and data. Enable snapshots per agent version; state needed across idle periods should be stored externally.

...

Operate: Govern and continuously improve

Production readiness means understanding how agents behave after deployment, and using that evidence to improve them. At Ignite, we’re connecting production insights, expert feedback, and optimization through continuous improvement in Foundry:
* Insights — GA: Identify recurring issues across production traces, see supporting evidence, and investigate likely causes. This visibility also extends to agents built with LangGraph, LangChain, and CrewAI.
* Annotations on traces — Public preview: Capture expert feedback on what worked, what didn’t, and what the agent should have done. Evaluation datasets, in preview, turn those reviews into reusable tests for future versions.
* Insights to Agent Optimizer — Preview: Send a recurring production issue to Agent Optimizer to generate candidate fixes and test them against your evaluations.

After a week of customer calls, ask Copilot to turn your meeting notes into a customer-ready FAQ in Word. Then open the document in Word to refine it, with the context from your notes already included. You can also turn your notes into a project timeline in Excel or a proposal in PowerPoint. results.title: Hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service at Ignite 2026: from pilot to production inside your enterprise boundaries | Microsoft Foundry Blog
excerpts:
Can it run on the Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) clusters we already operate? And what happens when a two-hour job gets interrupted?
At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re announcing a solution to each of these challenges for hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service. Below you’ll find what’s new, what you can use today, and what’s still to come. The egress and private CA updates apply to managed hosted agents, the ones Foundry runs for you; BYO-AKS support will be documented separately.

At a glance

* What’s new | What it means for you | Status
* Shared subnet IPs | Run many more sessions from the same subnet; your session quota still applies | Generally available (GA)
* Private CA trust | Call internal services that use your company’s certificates, with certificate checks still on | Public preview
* Network egress controls | One place to decide where an agent can connect, enforced outside the agent | Generally available (GA)
* Azure Policy governance for egress | Admins require compliant egress settings across a subscription or resource group | Public preview, starting in three regions
* Deploy hosted agents to your own AKS clusters | Foundry’s agent runtime on your own AKS cluster | Public preview targeted for early December
* Long-running resilient execution | Opt-in recovery for long jobs after a crash or redeploy | Generally available
* Configurable idle timeout | Sessions can wait from 2 minutes to 4 hours between requests | Generally available
* Memory snapshots | Faster cold starts for agents with heavy startup | Public preview

Scale: run far more sessions from the subnet you already have (GA)

If you run hosted agents in your own virtual network, each session used to take its own IP address from your delegated subnet. A /24 topped out at about 250 concurrent sessions, and teams with a tight IP plan hit that wall fast.
Hosted agent sessions now share subnet IP addresses. Each session still runs in its own VM-isolated sandbox. What changes is how far your subnet goes: our planning estimate for a /24 is now about 60,000 concurrent sessions, and even a /27, the smallest supported size, is planned for about 7,500. IP sharing is on for everyone, with no request needed.
These are planning estimates, not guarantees, and we still recommend a /24 or larger for production so there’s room for upgrades and maintenance. For most teams, your regional session quota is now the practical ceiling: by default 2,000 or 1,000 concurrent sessions per subscription, depending on the region. You can ask for more through a support request.
Status: Generally available now. See subnet size and concurrent sessions .

Trust: call internal services that use your company’s certificates (public preview)

Internal MCP servers, APIs and model gateways often use certificates from a private certificate authority (CA). Agents didn’t trust them, so calls failed, and the tempting fix was turning off certificate checks. Security teams don’t like that fix, for good reason.
Now you register your CA once on the Foundry resource. The CA certificate lives in Azure Key Vault, and every project in the resource picks it up. Certificate and hostname checks stay on, public CAs stay trusted, and you don’t bake CA files into container images or recreate project capability hosts.
Trust covers two paths. Tools, toolboxes and bring-your-own-model gateways use your CA in projects on your own virtual network, usually within a minute of the update. Hosted agent code that calls internal services directly trusts your CA in new sessions. The docs list what isn’t covered yet, such as remote builds and mutual TLS.
Status: Public preview. See Connect agents to services that use a private certificate authority .

Control: network egress controls are generally available (GA)

A tool list isn’t a network boundary. Agent code can start a subprocess, a library can follow a redirect, and generated code can call anything. Security teams want one place to say “these hosts, nothing else.”
Network egress controls for hosted agents are now generally available.

* Durable Task SDKs & Durable Task Scheduler | GA: Durable Extension for Microsoft Agent Framework, Customer-managed keys (CMK), Private endpoints Preview*: Durable execution for LangGraph & Pydantic AI, Native disaster recovery, Task Queues, Durable Task SDK for Go | GA & Public Preview * | DTS Ignite blog · Agent Framework blog · Go SDK

* Language runtimes & workers | GA: Golang on Flex Consumption, .NET 11 Preview*: Python 3.15 (Rust worker transport), Node.js 26 | GA & Public Preview * | Go docs · .NET 11 blog · Python 3.15 blog · Runtimes matrix
* Developer CLI & diagnostics | Azure Functions CLI (v5) and Azure Functions Network Troubleshooter v2 | Public Preview * | CLI docs · CLI repo · Network Troubleshooter blog

Trigger functions from SaaS events and call enterprise APIs with Managed Connectors

Managed Connectors in Azure Functions (GA)

Managed Connectors in Azure Functions is now generally available together with Azure Connector Namespace (also GA), supporting .NET isolated, Python, and Node.js.
Triggering functions from SaaS events or calling systems such as SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, GitHub, Jira, or ServiceNow previously required custom OAuth token refresh code, webhook registration, and public inbound callback endpoints.

...

Support for containers and deployment validation on Azure Functions Flex Consumption

OS-level dependency support via containers for Azure Functions Flex Consumption (Public Preview*)

We now support custom containers on Azure Functions Flex Consumption. Previously, needing OS-level packages such as headless Chromium for HTML-to-PDF rendering, GnuPG for payload encryption, custom fonts, or native dependencies meant moving off Flex Consumption to a full custom-container plan where you also had to patch the Functions host.
With Flex Consumption's worker-only container model, you package your app, one language worker (.NET 10/11 isolated, Python 3.13–3.15, Node.js 24, or Go 1.27), and any OS binaries inside a Linux container image while Azure operates and patches the Functions host, trigger listeners, and scaler outside your container.

...

Deployment validation logging in audit mode on Flex Consumption

Flex Consumption also introduces improved deployment logging with pre-production deployment validation in audit mode (enabled by default). On every code deployment, the platform spins up an isolated validation worker to verify that your package starts cleanly and registers valid triggers, logging a summary of discovered functions (name, language, and binding types/directions) to Kudu deployment logs and Application Insights traces . If a package fails to initialize or produce valid triggers, the deployment still proceeds via the standard deployment path without blocking—while emitting an actionable warning in the deployment log with the failure reason, deployment ID, and troubleshooting guidance so you can catch broken packages at deploy time rather than discovering silent failures later in production.

...

Agentic functions, bindings, and AI-assisted development

These announcements cover both sides of building with AI on Azure Functions: invoking skills and agents from Python functions at runtime, and using AI coding assistants to scaffold, modernize, test, and deploy function apps across languages.

As organizations are scaling AI adoption at an unprecedented pace, they need to stay in control of their data, operations, and access as regulatory and operational requirements evolve. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud gives them that control, with choice across public and private cloud environments. At Microsoft Frontier Tour last month, we highlighted how Sovereign Private Cloud , build in Azure Local, brings Azure infrastructure, services, and AI capabilities in customer-controlled environments.
At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we're building on that foundation with the general availability of Foundry Local, confidential virtual machines, and GitHub Enterprise Local, on Azure Local, along with public previews for agentic AI, connected to disconnected operations, and local data services. These announcements expand what organizations can build and run in their own sovereign environments, while keeping control over where data resides, who can access it, and how systems are operated, even when fully disconnected.

Sovereign AI in customer-controlled infrastructure

Foundry Local is now generally available on Azure Local. Organizations can deploy and run AI models close to their data, enabling local inference in connected and disconnected environments while maintaining control over their infrastructure, data, and operations.
We’re also expanding Foundry Local beyond model inference to support agentic AI scenarios on Azure Local. This release includes:
* Model catalog: Run AI models locally from an expanding model catalog, keeping inference close to data, applications and operations.

...

Confidential computing on Azure Local

Confidential VMs powered by AMD SEV-SNP are now generally available on supported AMD EPYC processors, providing hardware-backed memory encryption and attestation to help protect sensitive workloads while running. We're also expanding hardware choice with Intel TDX-based confidential VMs in preview on Intel Xeon processors.

Resilience and operational independence on Azure Local

We’re enabling organizations to move their Azure Local management control plane without redeploying infrastructure, migrating data, or interrupting running workloads . Virtual machines, AKS clusters, applications, and storage remain in place while management transitions to a new control plane.
The ability to move from connected-to-disconnected deployments (in preview ), allows customers to transition existing Azure-connected deployments to locally managed, disconnected environments.

Data services on Azure Local

Building on SQL Server support, we're expanding local data services for modern applications and AI workloads:
* SQL Server is generally available on Azure Local: Run enterprise database workloads on customer-controlled infrastructure across connected and disconnected environments.
* DocumentDB is in preview on Azure Local: Support document-oriented applications with local database capabilities.
* Blob Storage is in preview on Azure Local: Store and access unstructured data with cloud-native object storage while keeping data local.
Together, these services enable organizations to build data-driven and AI-powered applications while keeping sensitive information within their environments.

Sovereign developer workflows with GitHub Enterprise Local

GitHub Enterprise Local , now generally availability, brings GitHub Enterprise Server into Azure Local as a prebuilt virtual appliance. Repositories, CI/CD workflows, and development artifacts stay within the organization’s infrastructure and security boundaries, in both connected and disconnected environments.
In connected environments, developers can use GitHub Copilot with locally hosted repositories. In disconnected environments, Foundry Local enables AI-powered development using locally hosted models.
This gives organizations flexibility to develop and manage applications across connectivity scenarios while maintaining control over their code and infrastructure.

Ignite 2026: What's new in Microsoft Defender & Sentinel

Caroline_Lee's avatar
Caroline_Lee
Icon for Microsoft rank Microsoft
Nov 17, 2026
At Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re announcing new innovations across Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel that bring security operations and threat protection closer together, help organizations get ahead of attacks, secure AI agents and strengthen protection across critical workloads.
* The foundation for agentic security: Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender now includes the full breadth of SIEM capabilities and 90-days of built-in Defender data.
* Protection before the patch : Vulnerability shielding in Defender autonomously protects exposed systems before and during active attacks, giving security teams more time to deploy permanent patches to vulnerabilities.
* Protect AI agents wherever they run: Manage security posture for third-party agent platforms, prevent device code phishing and extend runtime protection for local AI agents on Windows.
* Protect people where they work: Extend defenses against browser-based attacks, malicious QR codes in Teams, and synthetic media threats.
Together, these innovations build on a shared foundation of signals, actuators, and coordinated response to help security teams move faster and stop attacks before they spread.

The foundation for agentic security

ISOC now includes the full breadth of SIEM capabilities and 90 days of built-in retention

The integrated SOC brings SIEM and threat protection together to provide the foundation for the agentic SOC. It gives people and agents shared context and the ability to see, understand, and act across the environment, so the security stack works as one system.
Building on the September 23 announcement , core ISOC capabilities in Microsoft Defender are now generally available, including case management, playbooks, workbooks and UEBA. Workspace creation and third-party ingestion are also generally available. In addition, we are expanding the preview to include the full breadth of SIEM capabilities for eligible Defender customers, while enabling existing Sentinel customers to opt into ISOC.
“What excites us most about ISOC is having a single pane of glass for security operations. Bringing SIEM and XDR together simplifies the analyst experience, while giving us an opportunity to optimize ingestion and automation costs.”
- Farhan Nadeem, Senior Security Officer, Government of Nunavut
New capabilities available in preview include 90 days of built-in Defender data retention, SOC optimization recommendations, Content Hub, detections as code, and automation audit logs.
Figure 1. The Defender home dashboard showcasing the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) experience

Simplify and scale security analytics with ingest-time data normalization

Security data comes from diverse sources and formats, making analysis at scale complex. To simplify this, Microsoft is introducing ingest-time normalization, which standardizes data at time of ingestion, thereby simplifying queries, improving performance, and enabling reuse across detections, investigations, threat hunting, analytics, and agentic scenarios. This helps teams spend less time managing data, and more time stopping threats. It is now available in preview.
Figure 2: Data normalization via parser management for query-ready security analytics.

Protection before the patch

AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploitation. In October 2026 alone, 1,413 CVEs were disclosed, marking it the largest Patch Tuesday on record. Attackers can exploit vulnerabilities within hours, while organizations often need days or weeks to patch. That gap creates a critical window of exposure.
Vulnerability shielding in Microsoft Defender, now in preview, helps close that gap by protecting vulnerable systems until patches are deployed.
On by default in Microsoft Defender, vulnerability shielding applies targeted, temporary protection to vulnerable systems in the gap between exposure and remediation, buying defenders time before they can apply a permanent patch.

...

Assess posture for agents on third-party platforms

Defender is extending security posture assessment to agents built on Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini, Google Vertex AI, and Anthropic Claude.
Now in preview, they appear in the same AI agent inventory as your Microsoft Copilot Studio and Microsoft Foundry agents, with risk assessments and security recommendations, so you can prioritize risk across platforms. Bring them into scope by connecting their platforms to Agent 365 through connected platforms .
Figure 4. Agent profile with security posture for Amazon Bedrock Agent

Protect local agents at runtime

Building on local AI agent discovery , runtime protection for local agents is now generally available* on Windows. Defender inspects critical points in the agent loop and can block malicious instructions before the agent acts. Supported agents include Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenClaw, ChatGPT Desktop (Chat) with the full list here .
Each detection raises an alert with agent and session context, correlated into cases for your SOC; in Block mode, Defender also stops the action and notifies the user.

Protect AI agents from attacks on trusted identities

excerpts:
1. Build modern and AI-powered applications with Redis 8 (Public preview)
Build semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), recommendations, and agent memory with new vector capabilities in Redis 8. Richer queries, atomic JSON updates, field-level expiration, and fine-grained security give developers additional ways to work with application and AI data.
For applications that combine structured data with vector search, these capabilities expand what you can query and manage within Azure Managed Redis.
Learn more about Redis 8: aka.ms/amr-redis8
2. Apply Redis best practices with Azure Managed Redis agent kit (Public preview)
Bring Redis and Azure best-practice guidance into your AI-assisted development workflow. The Azure Managed Redis agent kit provides recommendations for client configuration, resilience, performance, and Azure deployment, alongside guided migration workflows.
For example, use the guidance to review client configuration and resilience choices as you prepare an application for production. The kit supports development and operational decisions; it is not an agent runtime.
Explore the agent kit announcement: aka.ms/amr-agent-kit

Simplify migration and database caching

3. Azure Cache for Redis to Azure Managed Redis Migration Tooling (General availability)
Built-in DNS migration tooling helps reduce application configuration changes when moving from Azure Cache for Redis to Azure Managed Redis. Redirect an existing cache hostname to an Azure Managed Redis instance, with optional data retention to support migration.
For teams managing existing applications, hostname redirection simplifies one part of the cutover: changing where applications connect while retaining the hostname they already use.
Learn more about this announcement: aka.ms/amrmigrationtooling
4. Implement database caching patterns with integration guidance (General availability)
Choosing what to cache is as important as adding a cache. Database integration guidance provides caching patterns, reference architectures, and tutorials for applications using Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL.
Start with frequently requested database data, then use the guidance to evaluate a caching approach that can reduce repeated database requests and improve application responsiveness.  Each guide has a fully deployable sample app to help you get started adding Azure Managed Redis into your database-backed apps.
Explore database caching guidance: aka.ms/amr-database-integrations

Operate with greater visibility and control

5. Investigate workload imbalances with shard-level metrics in Azure Managed Redis (Public preview)
Inspect memory usage, key counts, and replication health for individual shards using Azure Monitor telemetry.
When investigating performance, use this added detail to understand whether workloads are distributed unevenly across shards and identify potential hotspots for further investigation.
Explore the shard-level metrics update: aka.ms/redis/whatsnew
6. Control endpoint access with IP filtering in Azure Managed Redis (Public preview)
Control access to publicly accessible cache endpoints with firewall rules. Restrict connections to approved source IP addresses or Azure service tags.
For example, use approved application source IP addresses to narrow which clients can reach a public cache endpoint.
Explore the IP filtering update: aka.ms/redis/whatsnew

Context at the scale of your organization
